en: Of the dense, tangled forest.
On the gently rolling forked ridge,
Upon a rise no wider than a palm,
A reddish mist appeared,
And smoke rose beyond the crest.
Brightly coloured bundles
Marked where Kyzylsart lay.
Smoke streamed into the sky,
A white tent came into view,
With a bearskin and a white gyrfalcon,
And the horse of Black Giant could be seen.
When Chürök saw all this,
The poor woman rejoiced
And tears poured from her eyes.
The great healer Kyzylsart—
A star had stirred in the heavens at his birth;
His fathers and forefathers
Had been friends with the noble lord.
They had shared grains of white wheat,
And, vowing to stand by one another,
Had clasped the holy creed;
They had licked the edge of a sword
And sworn a solemn oath.
This was the great healer himself,
The cherished dark eye of those who awaited him;
Honouring the ancestral spirits, the poor man
Had arrived at just this time.
God had granted her wish:
For Külchoro, hero of heroes,
His helper had arrived.
Formerly my heir, Kutubiy,
Was precious in the eyes of my princely father,
And to my forefather who passed before
He was his own appointed heir,
A descendant of the modest line—
My mind is baffled and divided.
My moon-beautiful kinswoman,
I came expressly to see you;
When the leopard-like hero, mighty as a cliff,
When that grey-maned warrior died,
I came expressly to see
The orphaned boy and widowed wife,
And to find a means of helping
Külchoro, whom the spirits uphold.
Seeing the orphaned, the widowed, and the wretched,
My heart was burdened,
Yet my honour was greatly restored
And my exposed shame was covered.
What was severed in me was joined,
And my tiny soul rejoiced;
My eyes have seen the spring flowing down the slope,
And I have no regret.
Today I have seen Seytek, left by the great warrior,
And my heart is content.
The orphaned child and the widowed woman—
I have seen them all and have no regret.”
So saying, Kyzylsart
Threw back his mantle and folded his arms,
Rested his golden-bladed battle-axe
Against his right side,
And, crying “My soul’s friend!” aloud,
Stood sobbing and wailing.
Your noble kinsman Kyzylsart
Spoke these words,
While all wailed aloud in true grief,
And he continued speaking thus.
Kyzylsart had been his friend,
Known as a hero from the beginning;
His dear falcon-like eyes
Did not blink as they filled with tears.
His grey beard thinned with age,
And tears flowing from both eyes
Poured down his breastbone.
As Kyzylsart stood thus,
He addressed moon-faced Aichürök:
“Your noble beauty was like paradise,
But your days have passed in servitude,
And your life has dwindled to a mere handful.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow;
Your heart holds sorrow, your breast burning coals.
This foul world strides about,
Deceiving its mortal servants.
You have no strength to fight,
No power to wrestle;
You have been treated brutally.
Your days have passed in servitude,
And you have been made a lesser wife.
Now that I have come, my kinswoman,
Your broken arm has been bound
And your true honour covered.
The Külchoro for whom you prayed
Has grown to manhood and become a hero;
Every affliction has left him,
And he is restored to what he was before.
From Black Giant, the mighty champion,
Six fleet horses came,
And a letter no larger than a palm.
Grieving at the outrage, I heard bitter news:
I heard that Semetey,
My sworn friend unto the hereafter, was dead,
And all my ribs shattered together.
My upright back was broken;
It was as though God had struck me utterly.
I was parted from the one who was my support,
From my grey-maned lion,
My towering mountain collapsed,
And my dear friend lay fallen.
The smiting God had struck;
The twelve rearguards and forty scouts
Were broken at every ridge.
I was parted from the one who sustained me,
From my true friend and lion.
From broad Egypt came the word:
I heard that Semetey
Had departed from this world.
Would you have waited for me, my princely khan?
He was a broad ridge beyond six passes,
Who dwelt in the Ala-Too,
Whom no man could defeat in combat,
A lion born among the Kyrgyz.
Though women bear sons to men,
They said that among mankind
His like would never be born again.
You were the bridge laid across the river;
My bridge has broken and fallen.
It is this that I lament.”
So she cried out in anguish,
Your fierce but noble sister-in-law,
Wailing as she invoked the great warrior.
While Aichürök lamented thus,
The birches wept and the willows wept,
Every living soul that watched her wept,
The bristling lions wept,
And the black earth groaned and wept.
All who wept
Wept consumed by their own grief.
When a hero leaves a widowed wife,
This vain world lies desolate;
When a son remains without seeing his father,
When the river dries and leaves only its bed,
When darkness covers human eyes—
“This is calamity,” they cried.
The multitude wailed in an uproar;
Black Giant and Kyzylsart mourned
As though the leopard-like hero had died that very day.
It was as though they had dug the earth with mattocks,
Recited his funeral prayer with due honour,
And buried him with the congregation that day;
As though they had laid him in his coffin,
The nation groaned and the people clamoured,
As though carrying him to the grave.
Black Giant and Kyzylsart
Grieved, the two khans weeping;
The khan and all the people wept,
Their hearts deeply stirred
For the woman Aichürök,
As countless hardships loomed ahead.
Her black hair untouched by a comb—
Aichürök wept until she was spent
And spread it strand by strand;
Her precious hair, long as meadow grass,
She spread across her breast.
Your kinsman Kyzylsart—
When she saw Kyzylsart,
It seemed her precious sultan had died.
The people cried out and the nation stirred,
As though burying their great warrior that day.
She raised a piercing cry,
And her white face, lovely as a plane tree—
Alas for the frailty of woman—
She clawed and tore again and again.
Dark blood flowed where she tore,
And Aichürök’s strength departed;
Her pale complexion faded,
And the blood flowing from both cheeks
Poured down over her breast.
Blood streamed like water through a ditch,
And Aichürök’s strength departed.
Hear how she raised her wailing voice,
Lamenting for her vanished lord:
“A charger that would not tire in six months’ riding
You were, my princely khan.
A falcon that took the wolf when properly flown
You were, my princely khan.
If ten thousand rivers joined,
You were their confluence, my princely khan.
If ten thousand cliffs joined,
You were their mighty collision, my princely khan.
Of the heavens and the blue sky
You were the supporting pillar, my princely khan.
Among ravenous lion-warriors
You alone were supreme, my princely khan.
Those upon whom you fixed your gaze
You would subdue, my princely khan.
Those who faced you eye to eye you conquered—
A star stirred in the heavens,
And in one night she awoke a thousand times;
She nursed me on her pure white milk
And fed me grains of white wheat.
She had an amulet hung around my neck,
Lest the enemy’s wrath strike me,
And had me raised in tenderness.
She reared me to maturity and made me a hero,
Made me the equal of heroic sons,
And raised a clamour when I was born.
My venerable white-haired mother,
Should the khan’s only prince
Have cause to wander in desolation?
My mother in this dark day, where are our people?
When will the day come that we reach them?
Should a noble prince’s only son
Have cause to roam as an exile?
My ill-fated mother, where are our people?
Across the yellow, rolling uplands,
When will the day come to cross the ridge?
When will we return to the land
Of willow-lined Keng-Kol and broad Talas?
When shall I cross them, dear mother—
Kara-Buura and broad Chatkal?
When shall I see, dear mother,
Those highlands where our people summer?
When shall we return to the uplands,
To my inheritance from my father,
To my Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
To keep court and dwell among the mountains?
When shall we return to the people
Of my ancestral inheritance,
Who play orompoi and strike the ordo stones?
When shall we cross the ridges
Of the two passes, Küyük and Chakmak?
When shall the mighty Kyrgyz and the many Argyn
Camp together in their villages
And open their hearts to laughter?
When shall we pass through the Seven Valleys
And reach our inheritance?”
The people cried out and the nation wept,
And while the multitude stood thus,
The hero’s son, Er Seytek,
Heard rumours among the people,
And heard that his mother had come.
Then Er Seytek
Heard the tale from Külchoro:
He learned that Semetey, gone to the other world,
Had been his father.
He grew angry and darkened,
His threatening face turned grim;
His black eyes became bloodshot,
His bloodied face turned ashen,
His heart became a fire of burning coals.
If the fierce one turned in wrath,
He became a blazing flame.
He made ready all his weapons,
And the fiery young eagle,
Hung at his side a sword without a sheath.
He heard the voice of the grief-stricken woman Chürök
And was deeply distressed,
